placement.position_note: Interpretive placement on a GENERATED lot, not a recovered parcel. The lot geometry is the K7 plat module's — this project has never read Thompson's numbering off a sheet, and the side lot lines and the alley are conjectural even where the block face is not. The building stands 5.5 m back from its street edge, which is a typology for the period and not a measurement of this lot. The whole footprint — not its centre — is tested against the platted street corridors, against its own lot lines and against every other footprint in the dataset, so no invented building of this parcel stands in the roadway; clearing the roadway is not the same as standing on a recovered lot.

siding_exposure_m.note: INVENTED WITHIN A STOCK SET, NOT DERIVED. No source states the exposed face of any Chicago building's siding. The value is one of four period mill sidings — 4.5, 5, 5.5 or 6 in to the weather; this roof wears 6 in — dealt in this building's own parcel recipe: drawn from the set on this record's stable key, then advanced so that no roof of the parcel standing within 60 m hangs the same course. It is NOT keyed to a construction season the way the named buildings' stocks are: this record's 1835-01-01 is the programme's count-unit convention and not a date anything was built, so keying to it would deal every anonymous roof in the town one stock. The separation is the surface variety T-0049 reconstructs, not a claim about 1835. docs/LIBERTIES.md L148 owns the invention and the recipe half is recorded beside it, under `tools/siding_stock.py`.

This anonymous roof is the dwelling of an inferred carpenter's household (17 of 20 this layer infers): hh_inf_carpenter_south_17 in data/residents/households/. THE ROOF'S OWN EXISTENCE, POSITION AND FOOTPRINT REMAIN CONJECTURAL and are unchanged by the adoption; what the adoption adds is an argued occupant instead of an anonymous count-unit. The occupant is hypothesised from the town's demonstrable needs - the 1835 census of 3,265 people in 398 dwellings against the trades Andreas's 1833 roster names - and is not a person: no name is claimed and no figure is drawn.

lot_address.note: SEATED BY THE LOT-ADDRESS POLICY (docs/LOT-ADDRESS.md; liberty L216). The Lake Street notice prints a LOT AND A BLOCK — LOT No. 7, in block No. 16, one lot east of Haddock's Tavern, on Lake street, in the town of Chicago — which is the plat's own language and the strongest placement statement in the corpus; 6 printings, 1834-06-18 to 1834-11-19, 4 of them cited here as legible, claims chicago_democrat_1834_06_18#c006, chicago_democrat_1834_09_03#c005, chicago_democrat_1834_10_15#c006, chicago_democrat_1834_11_19#c010. THE ADDRESS IS WHAT THIS ROOF GAINS AND THE ONLY THING IT GAINS: its existence, its position, its footprint and every form value are the 665-roof programme's and are unchanged, its `function` still reads as the anonymous family the recipe dealt it, and no coordinate moved to seat this. THE NOTICE SAYS OF THIS LOT: a large dwelling-house; a fine well. The notice says 'There is on said lot a large Dwelling-House'. Four of the six printings carry the words unbroken. WHAT IS DRAWN AT THIS ADDRESS IS NOT THIS HOUSE: the roof standing on the lot is the 665-roof programme's own count-unit, dealt to the D3 family before this address resolved to anything, and its footprint is a 5.36 x 6.38 m one-room cottage. The source says LARGE and the fabric under the address does not answer to that word. The address is what this record gains; the fabric is unchanged and still conjectural, and the mismatch is stated rather than repaired by re-dealing the block's family mix — which is a second demonstration and is filed as its own ticket. NOT DRAWN, and T-0592 has now settled why. The notice's second structure is a well and it is documented as plainly as the house; what was missing was a rule to place it by, and the reason recorded here used to be an absence — 'the town has no well' — which described the model rather than the town. THE READING IS docs/RESEARCH/wells.md AND ITS ANSWER IS NOT A WELL. Chicago in July 1835 took its drinking water from the lake by cart: the Board of Trustees paid $95.50 on 10 November 1834 for the digging of ONE public well, in Kinzie's Addition, and after that the town was served by two-wheeled carts carrying a hogshead, filled by pail at the foot of Randolph Street and run off at a customer's door through a short leathern hose at five to ten cents the barrel (town_findings_andreas_v1#c012, #c013); the Chicago Hydraulic Company was not chartered until 18 January 1836 and its works were not finished until 1842 (#c014). No ordinance of this town requires, sites or pays for a well — the fire ordinances of 1833, September and October 1834 and the code of 5 August 1835 legislate wardens, bystanders and a bucket line and never the water in the buckets. So there is no density to deal a well class from, and inventing one would misdescribe the town more badly than leaving it with none. THE WELL STAYS DOCUMENTED AND ABSENT, on that argument rather than on an absence. It is one of only three wells this project can name in a town of 3,265 people, and the fact that G. Spring advertised it in all six printings, beside the size of his house, is the argument that a well was a thing worth mentioning rather than a thing every lot had. The notice ends 'For terms enquire of G. SPRING' and says NOTHING ELSE about him. He is the man to apply to, which is not a statement that he owned the lot, and is certainly not a statement that he lived in the house — the same G. Spring is the attorney whose office the papers put second door west of the corner of Franklin and South Water. So this house is not named for him, and the register's business_g_spring is not moved here. T-0412 is the same trap read from the other side: a building offered FOR SALE must not mint a placement on its vendor. THE ADDRESS IS READ; WHERE THE ADDRESS LANDS IS THE BOTTOM TIER, and the chain is short enough to state in one breath. The words 'lot 7, block 16' are a direct reading of four printings. The block number is `inferred` — three blocks counted east of the one numeral the Wright sheet shows (data/traces/thompson_block_numbering.json). The lot number is `conjectural` twice over: four lots to a block face is a reading of one block, the lot lines it numbers are the plat module's and are drawn from no sheet, and the counter-clockwise scheme itself was read off block 18. A chain is as strong as its weakest link, so which committed roof stands at this address is graded at the bottom tier — the same grade the roof already carried, and it does not rise because a documented address was put on it.

what_it_supplies: that a named trade was being carried on in Chicago in a named week, and often where
self-reported addresses, which are the strongest address evidence this project has: the advertiser was paying, and his customers had to find him
dissolution, removal and replacement notices — the only thing that keeps a documented business out of the 1835 town under the owner's ruling 3
post-office letter lists, naming residents by the hundred (ruling 1: a listed name mints a resident candidate, flagged letter_list_only)
the village and later town ordinances, printed complete — the 7 November 1833 code is the richest single item in the run
arrivals and clearances, which date the piers and the harbour as working structures
public notices that fix a building as a polling place, an auction site or a meeting place on a given day
the paper's own imprint, self-reported: the corner of South Water and Clark streets
twenty-one months of continuous weekly attestation ending three weeks before the scene date, including the issue printed on 1835-07-01
what_it_does_not_supply: any building's form, material, storey count, fenestration or dimensions — an advertisement describes a trade, not a building
the specific corner of any junction it names: 'on the corner of' does not say which of the four
anything at all from an engraving — see trap 1; the cuts are the printer's stock
proof that a business named in 1833 or 1834 still stood on 1835-07-01; that is ruling 3's survival liberty, and it is a liberty
an argument from silence, unless corpus.json shows the issues either side of the silence are both in the deposit
a reading that outranks a scan read of the same passage — see ruling 2 and the C. & I. HARMON case
a citation without an issue page and column

what_it_supplies: A 665-roof production target with independently reconcilable group, district, level, and construction totals.

District character, spacing, variation, finish, and chronology constraints for a July 1835 reconstruction.

what_it_does_not_supply: A surviving July 1835 building census or parcel-by-parcel roof register.

Authority to replace stronger building-specific evidence already represented in the dataset.
